newsitem.title: CHINA: FORECAST - China debt trading seen hit by new issue.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - China debt trading seen hit by new issue.

text.p: The slow sale of China's latest state debt issue and new measures by Beijing to control securities trading could deal a body blow to the country's state debt spot and repurchase markets, analysts said on Sunday.

In the next month or so, trading volume on both markets is likely to plummet, with prices for spot state debt contracts expected to fall and interest rates for repo contracts to rise firmly, they said.
A total of 40 billion yuan ($4.82 billion) of three-year tradable treasury notes was issued in May and will be listed on the Shanghai stock exchange and other state debt trading floors on Monday.
But by the end of its issue, underwriters in Shanghai had sold less than 60 percent of the new T-note, mainly due to a low annual coupon of 9.18 percent, industry sources said.

The coupon compares with an average annual yield of more than 10 percent for existing spot state debt contracts on the Shanghai bourse, which accounts for more than 95 percent of state debt trading turnover in China, they said.
"Slow sales of the new T-note will see it making a very poor debut when it is listed on Monday," said one state debt trader.
"We expect the note to trade below its face value of 100 yuan in the first few trading days after the listing," he said.
A second trader agreed, saying the expected poor debut would weaken sentiment on the spot state debt market.
"Prices of existing contracts, already hit by a liquidity outflow with investors transferring their money to the active stock markets, are expected to continue to fall," he said.
The existing three-year T-note contract maturing in August 1999, which closed at 108.58 yuan on Friday, could lose two or three yuan after the new issue was listed, traders said.
The state debt repo market would mainly be hit by Beijing's recent measures to check over-heated stock market trading, analysts said.
The measures include a ban on state banks trading on the repo market to prevent bank money flowing into the stock markets.
"The ban will reduce liquidity on the repo market by about half," a local banker said. "This will sharply reduce repo trading volume and sharply push up interest rates for repo contracts."
Daily turnover on the Shanghai state debt repo market stands at an average of around seven billion yuan and is expected to fall to around three to four billion yuan a day, analysts said.
The annual interest rates for the most active three-day and seven-day contracts could rise by about five percentage points each from the current level of around 10 percent, they said.

Beijing has also set up a central state debt depository, which will be responsible for holding, clearing and settling all state debt transactions, to check short-selling on the state debt repurchase market.
Traders said short-term support for the repo market was coming from the many new domestic A share issues, which were in turn increasing demand for funds.
So far this year, A shares with a total face value of around five billion yuan have been issued by nearly 100 firms in China on the Shenzhen and Shanghai stock exchanges.
